editorNote: Alex, the lead is Anthropic's draft AI safety bill, which sets out when the government could block a frontier model's release. Your interests in US politics and markets run through the paper too, from the IMF bond-yield warning to the White House press secretary's removal.

lead.headline: Anthropic pitches draft AI safety bill to US lawmakers
lead.dek: The proposal would limit when the government could block the release or use of powerful AI models, according to reports citing Politico.

body.text: Anthropic representatives have quietly pitched a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security to Capitol Hill lawmakers, Politico reported on Friday, citing three people with knowledge of the efforts.

The draft would let the government block a model's release or use only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people.
The risk must stem from a biological weapon, a model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack, according to Politico as reported by CNA.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects proposals in the company's 'Advanced AI Framework' and would require developers to test frontier models, be transparent about findings, and have them independently evaluated.

lead.whyThis: You work in product and follow AI closely, and this draft bill would set the terms for when frontier models can be blocked.
lead.whyItMatters: The draft sets out how a leading AI developer wants federal rules to govern the most powerful AI models, a debate that could shape future oversight in the United States.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: The Department of Commerce did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Politico's account rests on three unnamed people, and the bill's path through Congress is not described in the sources.

world.line: US tech news aggregator relays Politico's report that Anthropic pitched its own AI safety bill to lawmakers.
Singapore's CNA reports the quietly pitched draft bill, citing Politico and an Anthropic spokesperson's comments to Reuters.
Nigeria's Punch briefly reports that Anthropic is circulating a draft AI bill among US lawmakers.
Pakistan's Dawn stresses the lack of federal AI legislation and notes the judge-approval condition in the draft.
India's Business News Today highlights the draft's provisions for halts, independent testing and judicial suspension.

slots.headline: IMF warns of possible 'disorderly' spike in government bond yields
slots.dek: The fund cites inflation, high debt and AI-related borrowing at its annual meetings in Bangkok.

body.text: The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion as inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowing pressure sovereign bond markets.
Yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs from the Middle East conflict and expectations of tighter monetary conditions.
The report said the bond market is "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," and that a sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values.

At the Bangkok meetings, IMF member countries called for more support for countries facing short-term financing challenges from wars and high energy prices, saying economic risks remain tilted to the downside.
IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said the meetings were marked by "optimism and worry" about the global economic outlook.

slots.whyThis: The IMF's warning on bond yields ties together the markets and inflation stories you want to follow without the noise.
slots.whyItMatters: Sovereign bond yields affect government borrowing costs and asset values, and the IMF's warning links these markets to inflation, debt and energy prices worldwide.
slots.forYou: As someone tracking markets: the IMF warns that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, and a sharp rise would mark down asset values.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: The sources do not say whether a disorderly spike in bond yields will occur or when, only that the risk could rise.

sources.name: Aaj TV English News - Business & Economy

world.line: The economy outlet leads with the IMF's bond market warning, tying it to debt, inflation and AI-related borrowing.
Al-Monitor, via Reuters, emphasises calls for more support for countries hit by wars and high energy prices.

world.line: Aaj TV, from Pakistan, reports the same IMF member statement on financing pressures and downside economic risks.

slots.headline: India's Gen Z protests mount over voter roll revision and election official
slots.dek: Demonstrators defied a government ban on gatherings, and reports say the protests may be the largest street dissent in a decade.

body.text: Protests in India followed a revision of voter rolls by the Election Commission, which had listed nearly 980 million names, and people turned out in defiance of a government ban on gatherings.
Local media found more than 130 million people were struck off the rolls or threatened with deletion, but NPR said it had not been able to confirm those figures.
Gen Z-led protesters are demanding the resignation of the country's top election official, and tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed to stop them.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project has said street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade.

slots.whyThis: Mass protests in India over voter rolls are a major world story that sits outside your usual beats.
slots.whyItMatters: The protests challenge the government over voter eligibility in the world's largest democracy and mark one of the biggest tests of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's rule.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: NPR could not confirm the figure of more than 130 million people struck off or threatened with deletion from the rolls.

world.line: Frames the protests around a voter roll revision and a government ban on gatherings, with NPR noting it could not confirm key numbers.
Profiles Neha Bora as a prominent face of the Gen Z protests and highlights police detentions of activists.
Stresses the scale of the security deployment and the independent data showing a possible decade high in street protests.
Presents the protests as a predicament for Modi, with Gen Z youth pouring onto India's streets as dissent surges.

slots.headline: Trump removes White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after less than a week
slots.dek: Two US officials confirmed she is 'transitioning out'; Trump said he is in no rush to name a replacement.

body.text: US President Donald Trump has removed Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary, according to reports.
Two US officials confirmed on Friday that Zacharia was fired and is 'transitioning out' after serving for less than a week.
Her public debut at the podium, on October 13, drew criticism of her performance, including reliance on notes and several verbal slips.
Reports said she had acknowledged she did not pass a bar exam, and Trump said he is in no rush to name a new press secretary.

slots.whyThis: It is the biggest US politics story of the day and concerns who speaks for the White House.
slots.whyItMatters: The White House press secretary is the main public link between the administration and the press, so a rapid turnover in the role draws wide attention.
slots.forYou: As someone following US politics: the White House press secretary was removed after less than a week, and Trump said he is in no rush to name a new one.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Official reasons for the removal were not stated in the sources; one outlet described her as fired while others said she was leaving. Reports differ on whether she served less than five days or less than a week.

sources.name: World News, International News and Updates - HUM News English
Pakistan News - Daily Pakistan English News

world.line: Pakistani outlet reports the removal as a direct decision by Trump, framing it as a swift shake-up of the press office.
UK broadcaster BBC focuses on her departure less than five days into the job and the media criticism of her credentials.

slots.headline: Officials say order to limit Ukraine's Starshield came from White House
slots.dek: Two US officials and a Western official say the restriction was ordered from inside the White House, though who made the decision is unclear.

body.text: Two US officials and a Western official say the order to limit SpaceX's Starshield service for Ukraine came from inside the White House. The officials did not say who in the White House made the decision.

Ukrainian officials said military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working when mounted on fast-moving objects, affecting drones that rely on them for guidance. A person in Ukraine's Defence Ministry later said the receptors worked in motion only at speeds up to 100 mph.

Trump said neither he nor Elon Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access. Four Republican senators joined Democrats in asking the Pentagon whether its officials ordered the restrictions.

slots.whyThis: It is a US politics story about a White House decision affecting a defence technology service.
slots.whyItMatters: Ukraine's battlefield communications depend on a US-controlled satellite system, and the dispute raises questions about how far Washington can shape that support.
slots.forYou: As someone following US politics: two US officials say the order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside the White House, though they did not say who made the decision.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Who in the White House or Pentagon gave the order is not confirmed. Sources do not agree on whether the restriction was lifted fully or only partly.

world.line: Pakistani outlet frames the restriction as a White House order tied to Trump's pressure over Russian refinery attacks.
UK paper argues Ukraine and Europe rely heavily on a system subject to the US President's whims.
Indian outlet emphasises Trump's denial that he or Musk played a role in the Starlink loss.

slots.headline: Suspicious letters sent to Republican and Democratic lawmakers' offices under federal investigation
slots.dek: The FBI and Postal Inspection Service are tracing letters with unknown substances, most of which were intercepted before delivery.

body.text: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" sent to congressional and state election offices across the US.
Senators Susan Collins, Pete Ricketts, Ted Cruz and Mike Rounds confirmed their offices were among those targeted, and Collins's office said the letters were intercepted and no one was injured.
At least five Democratic senators' offices received suspicious letters, most of them intercepted before delivery, according to the BBC.
Ricketts said a powdery substance sent to his Omaha office was confirmed by police and the FBI as not harmful.
The New York Times reported the first incident on Thursday, amid reports of growing threats against election officials.

slots.whyThis: Suspicious letters sent to lawmakers' offices are a US politics story with a federal investigation attached.
slots.whyItMatters: The mailings target officials who run or oversee elections weeks before the US midterms, and officials say they are investigating them as a security matter.
slots.forYou: As someone following US politics: federal authorities are investigating the letters, and Senator Collins's office said they were intercepted and no one was injured.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Authorities have not said how many offices were targeted or who sent the letters, and the exact nature of the substances is not stated.

slots.headline: Tesla Unveils Roadster That Uses SpaceX Thrusters to Fly
slots.dek: Tesla says production of the second-generation Roadster will start in 2028, and no price has been announced.

body.text: Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled the second-generation Roadster at a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas.
During the demonstration, the car used thrusters to lift itself into the air and over other Tesla vehicles, and Tesla showed it accelerating from 0 to 60 mph in one second.
Musk said Tesla will build the vehicle in 2028, and the company has not named a price.
Musk said the car is not necessarily safety-optimized, and Wired noted it is likely to raise the eyebrows of federal regulators.

slots.whyThis: A car that uses rocket thrusters to fly is a consumer-tech story with a clear product angle.
slots.whyItMatters: The vehicle is a product claim from Tesla and Musk, and its safety and regulatory questions are raised in early coverage, so buyers and regulators will need to see the details.
slots.forYou: As someone following consumer tech: Tesla says the Roadster will be built in 2028 with no price named, and Wired noted it is likely to raise the eyebrows of federal regulators.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Pricing, production details and regulatory response are not confirmed; Tesla's top-speed figures and Musk's hopeful speed target are claims from the event.

world.line: The UAE's The National says Tesla's flying Roadster raises more questions than answers.

slots.headline: Apple's foldable iPhone Duo faces high demand and shipping delays
slots.dek: Apple says demand for the $2,000 iPhone Duo is extraordinary, and Hong Kong police have received over 100 reports of unauthorised card charges tied to pre-orders.

body.text: Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, a foldable phone with a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display, which uses Touch ID on the power button instead of Face ID.
Engadget priced the iPhone Duo at $2,000 and said all indications are that it will be in high demand and relatively short supply, with launch set for October 23.
Apple says demand for the iPhone Duo is extraordinary, and many customers saw shipping delays pushed from November to December, then to the end of January.
Hong Kong police have received more than 100 reports of unauthorised credit card transactions related to iPhone Duo pre-orders, according to the South China Morning Post.

slots.whyThis: A new foldable iPhone with high demand and shipping delays is a consumer-tech story that a product manager will want to read.
slots.whyItMatters: Readers considering a new flagship phone, or anyone using online pre-orders, will see how availability and payment issues are unfolding.
slots.forYou: As someone following consumer tech: the iPhone Duo uses Touch ID on the power button instead of Face ID, and Apple says demand is extraordinary, with shipping delays pushed to the end of January.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: The articles do not confirm the cause of the unauthorised transactions or how many total pre-orders were placed.

world.line: Engadget, a US outlet, calls the iPhone Duo Apple's most exciting device in a decade while noting its high price and missing Face ID.
The South China Morning Post reports Hong Kong police complaints about credit card charges linked to the pre-orders.
Indian coverage highlights reports of sell-outs in China and delivery delays pushed into next year.

offYourBeat.headline: Over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, UNICEF says
offYourBeat.dek: UNICEF says the truce between Israel and Hamas has not protected children, with seven more reported killed in the past two weeks.

body.text: UNICEF said on Friday that more than 340 children have been reported killed in Gaza since a ceasefire was announced a little over a year earlier.
UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said that in the last two weeks, five boys and two girls were reported killed and at least 33 children were seriously injured.
UNICEF said children were hit by air strikes, drone strikes and gunfire, and hundreds more have been injured since the ceasefire.
Pires said, "For families mourning the loss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire."

offYourBeat.whyThis: UNICEF's figures on children killed in Gaza since the ceasefire are an important world story that is worth knowing.
offYourBeat.whyItMatters: The figures describe continuing child casualties in Gaza despite a ceasefire, a situation that UN agencies are reporting on.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: The figures are reported by UNICEF and have not been independently verified in these sources. The sources do not specify the exact number of injured beyond hundreds.

world.line: The UN News piece, from Geneva, quotes UNICEF's own spokesperson on the child toll since the ceasefire.
Pakistani outlet HUM News frames the UNICEF report as showing the truce has failed to shield children from the conflict.

offYourBeat.headline: Trump cancels livestream of Fort Hood shooter's firing squad execution
offYourBeat.dek: The president overruled the defense secretary's plan, while the execution of Nidal Hasan will still proceed on December 3 with families able to attend in person.

body.text: US President Donald Trump said he had canceled the planned livestream of the execution of Nidal Hasan, saying he overruled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who had intended it to be broadcast.

Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was found guilty in a military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, and he is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3.
Trump wrote on social media that the execution 'will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,' and said immediate victims' families may view it in person.
A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals and other senior officers had called the livestream a 'barbaric abuse of authority' in an open letter.

offYourBeat.whyThis: It is an off-beat pick on a US execution and a presidential decision that overruled the Defense Secretary.
offYourBeat.whyItMatters: The decision shapes how the US carries out executions and reflects a debate over public spectacle, justice and the treatment of a mass killer.
offYourBeat.forYou: As someone following US politics: Trump said he overruled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the livestream, and the execution is scheduled for December 3.

briefs.headline: Pope Leo XIV recovers in Rome hospital after lung cancer surgery
briefs.dek: The Vatican says the 71-year-old pope is recovering well and is expected to leave hospital after four days, pending further tests.

body.text: Pope Leo XIV had part of a lung removed on Tuesday for lung cancer. Vatican doctors said a chest X-ray showed a good recovery of the operated lung.
The Vatican released photos of the pope celebrating mass on Friday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is recovering.
Sky News reported the Vatican said the pope is set to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery. Further tests will determine whether he is cancer-free or needs more treatment.

briefs.whyThis: One of today's most-covered stories: 11 outlets.
briefs.whyItMatters: The pope leads more than 1.4 billion Catholics, so his health and any changes to his schedule draw wide public attention.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: It is not yet known whether the pope is cancer-free or will need further treatment. The Vatican had not said whether he would lead the Sunday Angelus from hospital or from the Vatican.

briefs.headline: US wholesale and consumer inflation climb faster than expected in September
briefs.dek: Energy costs tied to the war with Iran drove much of the increase, weeks before the midterm elections.

body.text: US wholesale prices rose 1.3% in September from August and 6.3% from a year earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
Energy prices, pushed higher by conflicts including the war with Iran, accounted for 80% of a 2.9% jump in goods prices.
Consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September, above the 3.6% that analysts had expected.
The Social Security Administration said benefits will increase next year to help keep pace with rising living costs.
Overall US import prices rose 1.1% in September, after a 0.5% rise in August.

briefs.whyThis: Matches your interest in the global economy; 7 outlets are covering it.
briefs.whyItMatters: Higher prices affect household budgets and set the size of Social Security increases, and the data comes just before the midterm elections.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Sources give different release days for the wholesale and consumer reports, and the reports do not give a full explanation beyond energy costs.

briefs.headline: Tech share sell-off spreads from Seoul to Wall Street
briefs.dek: Chip and AI-linked stocks fell sharply in Asia and the US as inflation and interest-rate fears grew.

body.text: South Korea's Kospi 200 fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that halted trading at points, with SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down nearly 11% and 9.5%.
Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 4.9% on Thursday, after Kioxia fell 11% and SoftBank, an investor in OpenAI, fell 10%.
Software and semiconductor stocks, which have not moved together much this year, collectively fell on Friday as AI and interest-rate fears hit the market.

briefs.whyItMatters: Sharp moves in AI-linked and chip stocks reflect broader worries about inflation and interest rates that can affect markets worldwide.

everyonesFrontPage.dek: Brent fell to $105.21 a barrel as traders weighed Strait of Hormuz flows and possible US sanctions easing on shadow fleet tankers.

The International Energy Agency agreed to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market, and a US official said the Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some shadow fleet vessels.
OPEC projects global oil demand to average 108.2 million barrels per day in 2027, up from 105.8 million in 2026, with India and non-OECD Asia leading growth.

everyonesFrontPage.headline: Trump waives Russia sanctions and tariffs days before they were due
everyonesFrontPage.dek: The executive order, signed as Trump and Zelensky traded sharp words, suspends penalties tied to Russia's oil and gas revenues.

body.text: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The measures, known as the Lindsey Graham Act after the late senator who sponsored it, were signed into law in September and allowed tariffs of up to 100% on the top buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The White House order said the waiver was in the national interest of the United States, which prompted a backlash from US lawmakers, according to reports.

The move came as relations between Washington and Kyiv soured after a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel, and analysts said the new measures could have raised oil prices before the midterm elections.

everyonesFrontPage.whyThis: One of today's shared front-page stories, shown to every reader.

trust.label: confirmed
trust.unknowns: Reports do not say how long the waiver will last beyond a statement that it remains in effect until Trump or his top officials determine otherwise.
